extra.message: Text returned from a retrieval/RAG lookup is concatenated into an LLM message body without going through a delimiting, escaping, or provenance-tagging step first. Retrieved documents are attacker-reachable in most RAG deployments (anyone who can get content into the corpus, or compromise a source the corpus indexes, controls this text). Mixed untagged into the same message the model treats as instructions, this is the classic indirect prompt injection setup: the model has no structural signal that this text is "reference data" rather than "things to obey." Wrap retrieved content in an explicit, consistently-applied delimiter or data-marking scheme (OWASP LLM01:2026 mitigation #6) and keep it out of the instruction channel, or treat it as untrusted input and re-validate any instruction-like content it contains before use.

metadata.note: Intraprocedural only (Semgrep OSS limit). This rule only sees a source and sink inside the same function. If a project's retrieval call and its message-assembly step live in different functions, this rule will not connect them; that requires Semgrep Pro's interprocedural taint analysis.

extra.message: Arguments parsed from a model-issued tool call are passed into a dynamically-selected tool implementation without first going through an authorization/policy check. An LLM agent's decision to call a tool (and the arguments it supplies) can be steered by anything the model has read, including an indirect prompt injection from a retrieved document or a tool result. OWASP LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency's top mitigation is to implement authorization in deterministic application logic, not to rely on the model to decide when a call is appropriate. Route the parsed arguments through an authorize()/permission-check call (and fail closed on denial) before invoking the tool implementation.

owasp: LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency (was LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency)
metadata.note: Intraprocedural only (Semgrep OSS limit): the taint source (parsed tool-call arguments) and the sink (the dynamic call site) must be in the same function. Separately, note the pattern-not-inside comment on the sink below: Semgrep taint-mode pattern-sanitizers only clear a variable that gets reassigned to a "clean" value, not a variable whose use is merely gated by an if/else after a bare authorization call, so this rule uses a structural exclusion instead of a taint sanitizer to avoid flagging the real target's correctly-authorized branch. That exclusion recognizes exactly one code shape (an authorize()-style call followed by the dispatch call in the same block) and may miss or misjudge differently structured checks.

extra.message: The return value of a tool call is serialized and appended back into the conversation the model reads, with no trust tiering, size limit, or content check applied first. Tool results are a second indirect injection surface distinct from RAG retrieval: any tool that reaches external or attacker-influenced data (a file, an API response, another user's input) can hand the model text that looks like an instruction, and that text goes straight back into the same message stream the model treats as authoritative on the next hop. Treat tool output as untrusted the same way retrieved documents are treated; apply a trust tier, size cap, or content filter before appending it to the conversation.

cwe: CWE-1426: Improper Validation of Generative AI Output
metadata.note: Intraprocedural only (Semgrep OSS limit). Confidence is LOW rather than MEDIUM because "tool result appended as a message" is also the normal, correct shape of a tool-calling agent loop; this rule cannot tell whether the tool's own source data is trusted (e.g. a read-only lookup of non-sensitive local config vs. a fetch of arbitrary external/user-controlled content), which is exactly the kind of judgment call OSS taint analysis, which sees code shape and not data provenance, cannot make on its own.

extra.message: SCOPE NOTE, READ BEFORE ACTING ON THIS FINDING: this rule can only check a path-read call and any containment check that appear in the SAME function. The realistic version of this vulnerability has the path parameter accepted in one function (e.g. a tool implementation like read_file()) and the containment/allow-list check enforced by a caller in a different function or module (e.g. an authz layer invoked from the agent's dispatch loop before the tool runs). Semgrep OSS taint mode cannot see across that call boundary ("Interprocedural taint analysis is a Semgrep Pro feature" per Semgrep's own docs), so a tool function that itself does no validation will always look unchecked to this rule, REGARDLESS of whether a caller elsewhere already enforced containment. In this project's own target, that is exactly the real shape: tools.py's read_file() takes a raw path with no check of its own, and the actual containment check lives in authz.py, called from main.py, neither of which read_file() itself references. Expect this rule to fire on every tool function that reads by path and validates nothing locally, whether or not the overall system is actually safe. Use Semgrep Pro's interprocedural taint mode, or manual review of the call sites, to determine whether an external check actually gates the call before treating a finding here as a confirmed vulnerability.

cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
owasp: LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency (was LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency)
metadata.note: DELIBERATELY LIMITED SCOPE. Only sees a containment/normalization check if it happens inside the same function as the lookup. In this project's target the real containment check (authz.py's check_read_file, using PurePosixPath and .parents) is enforced by a caller in a different module entirely, so this rule cannot observe it and will flag tools.py's read_file() regardless of whether the caller gates it. That is intentional: it demonstrates the boundary rather than hiding it behind a rule that looks more capable than it is. Confirming whether a given path-accepting function is actually protected requires tracing its callers by hand or with Semgrep Pro. Also note: a bare `authorize(...)` call that only gates a branch via if/return, without reassigning the path variable to a "clean" value, does not register as a Semgrep taint-mode sanitizer at all (sanitizers only clear a variable that gets reassigned to match the sanitizer pattern). This rule uses a pattern-not-inside structural exclusion for that shape instead, which recognizes exactly one code layout (an authorize()/check_read_file() call followed by the lookup, textually in the same block) and can still miss a differently structured guard.
